content:
After the man was found gathering sticks on the Sabbath and was put to death, Yahweh immediately gave Israel the command to wear tassels on the corners of their garments. The purpose was very practical. When the people looked at the tassels, they were to remember God's commandments and obey them. Today let us look more closely at these tassels, at the blue thread within them, at where they were placed, and at the beautiful truths that Yahweh hid inside this simple command.

This tassel is often called the tzitzit, a word that refers to a fringe, a tassel, or a hanging thread. These were attached to the four corners of the outer garment. The command is repeated in Deuteronomy 22:12, "Thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture." One important feature was the blue cord, for Numbers 15:38 specifically says that a cord of blue was to be placed in the tassel. This blue thread made the tassel visually distinctive, so that it would catch the eye. And the reason is given directly in Numbers 15:39-40. When the Israelites looked at the tassels, they were to remember all of Yahweh's commandments, do them, and not follow after their own hearts and their own eyes. So, the tassel worked almost like a visible reminder attached to the body, quietly saying, "Remember whom you belong to. Remember the covenant. Remember the commandments." The path it traced was simple: do not follow your own heart and your own eyes, but look at the tassel, remember Yahweh's commandments, obey them, and be holy to your God.

This also helps to explain a later practice we find in the Gospels. By the time Christ came, the Jews were still wearing these fringes. The New Testament uses the Greek word kraspedon, meaning the edge, the border, or the tassel of a garment. And Christ Himself apparently wore them, for in Matthew 9:20 the woman touched the hem, or fringe, of His garment, and the same word appears again in Matthew 14:36. Later Jewish tradition added a great deal of detail about the knots and how the threads were folded, but we will pause only on what the Torah itself says, and on the truths that Scripture makes plain.

The blue thread was not chosen at random. The Bible ties blue again and again to the sanctuary and to the priesthood. The Tabernacle curtains, the veil, and the high priest's garments were all rich in blue, and in fact the high priest's robe was made of blue (Exodus 26:1, 31; 28:31). So blue is the colour of the holy place, of the priesthood, of the heavenly. And Scripture lifts our eyes even higher, for when the elders of Israel went up the mountain, "There they saw the God of Israel. Under his feet there seemed to be a surface of brilliant blue lapis lazuli, as clear as the sky itself" (Exodus 24:10). So, the blue thread carries our gaze upward, from the garment to the heavens, up to the very throne of God.

The blue says to us: the commandments come down from heaven; keep your eyes lifted up to God; you are called to a heavenly holiness. The blue is the vertical line, joining earth to heaven.

Then there are the four corners, and these point in the opposite direction.
Where the blue points upward, the four corners point outward, to the whole earth and to the whole of life. The four corners are the Bible's own picture of the whole earth, of every direction. Yahweh promised to "gather the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth" (Isaiah 11:12). Ezekiel warned that "the end is come upon the four corners of the land" (Ezekiel 7:2). And John saw "four angels standing on the four corners of the earth" (Revelation 7:1). Four corners means totality, everywhere, all directions. So, the four corners say to us: God's commandments cover the whole of your life, every direction you turn, every corner of your walk, and the call of God goes out to the four corners of the earth, to all nations. If the blue is the vertical line reaching up to heaven, the four corners are the horizontal line reaching out across the whole earth and the whole man.

Now put the two together, for here is the heart of the teaching. The blue points up, to heaven, to the throne, to holiness, and to the priesthood. The four corners point out, to the whole earth, to every direction, to all of life, and to all nations. One is vertical, and one is horizontal. So, every single tassel was a small picture of a life joined to God above, in the blue, and covering everything below, in the four corners. Heaven and earth were held together in one simple reminder, telling the wearer to remember, to obey, and to be holy.

And here is a beautiful thread that runs straight to Christ, and it is solid in the Hebrew itself. The word for the corner of the garment in Numbers 15:38 and Deuteronomy 22:12 is kanaph, and this same word also means wing. Now hear the words of Malachi, "Unto you... shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings" (Malachi 4:2). The very word for the corner of the garment, where the tassel hangs, is the word for the wings where the Messiah carries healing. And that is exactly what the Gospels show us. The sick reached for the border of Christ's garment, the tzitzit, and they were healed. The woman with the issue of blood "touched the border of his garment" (Luke 8:44), and "as many as touched the hem of his garment were made whole" (Matthew 14:36). They were reaching for the tassel on the kanaph, the very wings where Malachi had promised that healing would be found. So, the whole type comes together. Christ wore the tassel like every faithful Israelite, and the healing in His wings was found at the very corner where the blue thread hung. Heaven's holiness, pictured in the blue, was reaching down to heal the whole earth, pictured in the four corners.

Let us close with one warning, and it comes from the mouth of Christ Himself.
The tassel was meant to turn the heart inward to obedience. But the Pharisees turned it into an outward show, for Christ said they "enlarge the borders of their garments... to be seen of men" (Matthew 23:5). They made their tassels large so that others would notice how religious they were. So, the lesson lands with a warning: the blue thread and the four corners mean nothing at all if they are worn merely for display. The point was never the thread itself. The point was always to remember, to obey, and to be holy (Numbers 15:40). A reminder worn for the eyes of men, while the heart forgets God, has entirely missed its purpose. Tomorrow, Yahweh willing, we will study the tassel of the New Creation, and what all of this means for us who belong to Christ.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God, enthroned above the brightness of the heavens,
We thank You for the blue thread that lifts our eyes upward to Your holiness and Your throne.

We thank You for the four corners, reminding us that Your Word covers the whole of our lives.

Join us to heaven above and let Your commandments cover every corner of our walk below.

We thank You that healing was found in the wings of Christ, where the blue thread hung.

Keep us from wearing our devotion for the eyes of men; let us truly remember, obey, and be holy.

"I lift my eyes to you, O God, enthroned in heaven." - Psalm 123:1

In Christ’s name, in whose wings is healing, we pray. Amen.
